title: Reversible reactions and equilibria
learningObjective: know that some reactions are reversible and this is indicated by the symbol ⇌ in equations; describe reversible reactions such as the dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate and the effect of heat on ammonium chloride; know that a reversible reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium in a sealed container; know that the characteristics of a reaction at dynamic equilibrium are: • the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate • the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.; understand why a catalyst does not affect the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction; know the effect of changing either temperature or pressure on the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction

sections.title: Reversible reactions and equilibria
sections.markdown:
Some chemical changes refuse to be one-way journeys. Heat a blue crystal
and it turns white; add water and the blue returns. Burn fuel and the
products sit there forever; but split ammonium chloride by heating and
the two products quietly recombine the moment they cool. A
[[reversible-reaction]] is a reaction whose products can turn back into
the original reactants — and once you start looking, you find them
everywhere in chemistry.

This chapter has one driving question. If a reaction can go both ways,
how do you arrange conditions so that the mixture ends up containing as
much as possible of the substance you want? That question runs the whole
chapter: first the idea of reversibility and its arrow, then what happens
inside a sealed container where the two opposing changes fight to a
stand-off called [[dynamic-equilibrium]], and finally how shifting
temperature, pressure or a catalyst moves that stand-off one way or the
other.

The chapter runs on two tracks. The **core track** (assessed in both
Paper 1C and Paper 2C) covers reversibility and the special double arrow
⇌ used in equations, plus two named reversible reactions in full: the
dehydration of hydrated copper(II) sulfate and the effect of heat on
ammonium chloride. The **chemistry-only track** (Paper 2C) builds on
that foundation: dynamic equilibrium in a sealed container, the two
characteristics that define it, why a catalyst leaves the position of
equilibrium untouched, and how changing temperature or pressure moves
the position of equilibrium in a predictable direction.

Two habits will carry you through. First, always ask "which direction?"
— for any change you make to a reversible reaction, the mixture responds
in a direction, and naming that direction precisely (towards reactants
or towards products) is the mark-earning skill. Second, keep the two
words in *dynamic equilibrium* separate in your mind: *dynamic* means
both reactions never stop, *equilibrium* means nothing overall changes.
Every exam answer in this chapter is built from those two halves.

:::prior-knowledge
You have met the pieces this chapter assembles: water of crystallisation
and crystal formulas (u1:c05 and u1:c06), the anhydrous copper(II)
sulfate test for water (u2:c18), exothermic and endothermic changes with
their ∆H signs (u3:c19), and the rates chapter's catalyst — the substance
that speeds a reaction up but is chemically unchanged at the end
(u3:c20). That last chapter matters more than usual here: equilibrium
questions constantly borrow ∆H signs and rate language, so revise u3:c19
before the temperature work in s07 if the sign conventions feel shaky.
:::

:::cross-curricular
"As much as possible of what you want" is the daily business of
industrial chemistry. Ammonia for fertiliser, sulfuric acid for almost
every manufactured product — both are made by reversible reactions where
engineers choose temperature and pressure to push the equilibrium towards
the product side. The economics of entire chemical plants ride on the
prediction rules you will learn in s06 and s07.
:::

:::misconception
"Reversible reactions are rare, special reactions." The opposite is true
once you know the sign. Any reaction where the products can meet each
other and re-react is potentially reversible, and the two examples this
chapter names in full — a salt crystal losing and regaining water, and a
white solid splitting into two gases that recombine on cooling — are
ordinary chemistry, not exotic cases. The reversible arrow ⇌ is the
everyday notation for them, not a rare warning sign.
:::

:::exam-hint
Specification wording you can quote: know that some reactions are
reversible and this is indicated by the symbol ⇌ in equations. Notice
the precise claim — the *symbol* indicates reversibility. If an exam
question shows an equation with ⇌ and asks what it means, one mark is
waiting for the statement that the reaction can proceed in both
directions, not a vague "it goes backwards".
:::

:::quick-check
Before moving on: can you define a reversible reaction in one sentence
and draw the arrow that shows one? Can you name the two tracks of this
chapter — which two reactions belong to the core track, and which four
specification statements belong to the chemistry-only track? If the
track split is fuzzy, reread the third paragraph — every later section
is labelled by which track it serves.
:::

sections.title: Dehydration of copper(II) sulfate crystals
sections.markdown:
Heat blue copper(II) sulfate crystals gently and something quietly
dramatic happens: the blue colour drains away, the crystals crumble into
a white powder, and water is driven off. The heating makes the crystals
lose their [[water-of-crystallisation]] — the water packed into the
crystal's structure — and what remains is white
[[anhydrous]] copper(II) sulfate. *Anhydrous* simply means *without
water*. No new substances entered the tube; the crystal gave up part of
itself, and that part was water.

Now reverse the film. Add water to the white solid and it turns blue
again — and it also becomes very warm. The rehydration releases heat
energy, which you can feel through the tube. The original change has
been exactly reversed: white back to blue, water restored into the
crystal structure, and the heat that went in on heating comes back out
on re-wetting. Every step of the forward change has a matching step in
the reverse direction.

This exact-reversal — including the heat — is what earns the reaction
its name and its special notation. This is called a
[[reversible-reaction]], and it is indicated in equations by a special
double arrow, ⇌, with half arrowheads pointing each way. The double
arrow is a compact promise: everything on the left can become
everything on the right, and everything on the right can become
everything on the left, under the right conditions.

Keep this reaction ready in your memory. It is one of the two named
examples the specification asks you to describe, and its colour change
makes it the chapter's built-in indicator: whenever a later section
needs a visible signal that an equilibrium has shifted, the blue-white
switch of copper(II) sulfate is the picture to hold. In s08 you will
meet its colour-based partner for gases — the brown-pale switch of
nitrogen dioxide — and the two together cover every equilibrium-shift
question the exam can colour-code.

:::misconception
"Heating drove the water out, so the crystal was destroyed." Nothing was
destroyed — the water of crystallisation is part of the crystal's
structure, not an impurity, and removing it is a chemical change that
can be undone completely. The evidence is in your hand: add water back
and the original blue solid returns, crystal structure rebuilt, with
the heat balance reversed just as exactly. Destruction would leave no
path home.
:::

:::exam-hint
A describe question on this reaction earns its marks in ordered
observations: blue crystals turn white on gentle heating (water driven
off, anhydrous white solid formed); adding water turns the solid blue
again and the tube becomes warm. The warmth is a mark-scoring
observation, not decoration — it is the evidence that the reverse
change is exothermic, and it connects this section directly to the ∆H
reasoning you will use on the chemistry-only track.
:::

:::quick-check
Cover the section and reconstruct it: what colour change happens on
gentle heating, what is given off, what does *anhydrous* mean, and what
two things happen when water is added back? If you can deliver all four
in order — blue to white, water driven off, *without water*, blue again
and warm — you own the first named reversible reaction of the
specification.
:::

sections.title: Two reversible reactions
sections.markdown:
The specification asks you to describe two reversible reactions in
detail, and they make a matched pair: one change driven by heat acting
on a solid crystal, one change driven by heat acting on a white powder
that splits into two gases.

**Reaction 1 — hydrated copper(II) sulfate.** On gentle heating the blue
crystals split into white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water; on
adding water the change runs backwards and blue crystals form again,
releasing heat. The forward direction needs heat supplied; the reverse
direction gives heat out. Both directions have been observed directly
in s02, and the equation carries the double arrow to show it:

CuSO4·5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l)

The classification matters as much as the observation. The forward
change — one substance broken into simpler substances by heat alone —
is an example of [[thermal-decomposition]]. Any time heat alone pulls a
compound apart, that word is available, and examiners like to see it
attached to this reaction.

**Reaction 2 — ammonium chloride.** Warm a tube containing white
ammonium chloride crystals and they vanish from the bottom of the tube
and reappear as a white solid further up, where the glass is cooler.
Heating ammonium chloride splits it into two colourless gases, ammonia
and hydrogen chloride. The equations tell the story in three lines.
Splitting needs heat:

NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g)  (heat needed)

The gases recombine further up the tube, where it is cooler:

NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s)  (heat released)

And because the whole thing reverses when the conditions change from hot
to cool, the summary equation carries the reversible arrow:

NH3(g) + HCl(g) ⇌ NH4Cl(s)

The recombination step is a reaction between an acid and a base:
hydrogen chloride is the acid and ammonia is the base, meeting to make
the white solid ammonium chloride. The two reactions also hand you the
chapter's directional vocabulary. In an equation as written, the
[[forward-reaction]] runs left to right and the [[reverse-reaction]]
runs right to left — and for the ammonium chloride system, which
direction runs depends entirely on whether the surroundings are hotter
or cooler than the reaction needs.

:::key-point
The forward change in the copper(II) sulfate reaction — one substance
broken into simpler substances by heat alone — is an example of thermal
decomposition.
:::

:::key-point
The recombination step of the ammonium chloride reaction is a reaction
between an acid (HCl) and a base (NH3), producing the salt ammonium
chloride.
:::

:::misconception
"The ammonium chloride disappeared, so it vaporised like dry ice."
Vaporising is a physical change — the substance would condense back in
the same place it left. Here the white solid returns in a *different
place* (further up the tube, where it is cooler) and only after its
molecules were split into two different gases and recombined. Movement
plus splitting plus re-forming is a chemical reversal, which is exactly
why this reaction is a named reversible reaction and not an evaporation
demo.
:::

:::exam-hint
Describe questions on heating ammonium chloride want the full narrative:
white crystals disappear from the bottom of the tube and reappear
further up; the solid splits into the colourless gases ammonia and
hydrogen chloride; the gases recombine where it is cooler. The mark
scheme's favourite discriminator is *where* the solid reappears and why
— cooler glass, further up — so tie the position of the new white solid
to the temperature change when you write.
:::

:::quick-check
From memory: write the splitting equation for ammonium chloride and say
which direction needs heat and which releases it. Then classify the
copper(II) sulfate forward change with its proper name. If you can also
state which gas is the acid and which the base in the recombination
step, the whole of the core track's reaction list is secure.
:::

sections.title: Reversible reactions in a sealed container
sections.markdown:
A [[sealed-container]] means that no substances are added to the
reaction mixture and no substances escape from it. Heat is different:
it may be either given off or absorbed — energy can cross the walls
even when matter cannot. That single restriction is what the
chemistry-only track's equilibrium story is built on, because a
reversible reaction can only show its full behaviour when both
substances and their products are trapped together.

Watch the behaviour with a model. Imagine a substance that exists in
two forms — one shown as a blue square, the other as a yellow square —
and suppose you start with a sample that is entirely blue. Because you
begin with a high concentration of blue squares, the rate at which they
turn yellow starts relatively high, counted as squares changing colour
per second. But as the blue gradually gets used up, that rate of change
falls. Meanwhile the yellow squares can also change back to blue — it is
a reversible reaction, so the products can react with each other and go
back to form reactants. At the start there are no yellow squares, so the
yellow-to-blue rate is zero; as yellow accumulates, the
yellow-to-blue rate rises.

Make the model numeric. Imagine you started with 64 blue squares, and in
any second there is a one-in-four chance of each of them changing
colour. In the first second, 16 change, leaving 48 blue. In the next
second a quarter of these change — but that is only 12, leaving 36 blue
ones. In the third second, nine change, and so on: 64, then 48, then 36,
then 27. The rate of change falls as the number — the concentration — of
blue squares falls. The same one-in-four rule drives the growing yellow
population in the opposite direction, so the falling blue-to-yellow rate
and the rising yellow-to-blue rate must eventually meet.

Soon the rates of both reactions become equal. At that point blue
squares are changing into yellow at exactly the same rate that yellow
ones are turning blue. What would you see? The total numbers of blue and
yellow squares remain constant — but the reaction is still happening.
Follow the fate of any one particular square and you find it is
sometimes blue and sometimes yellow, flipping back and forth forever.
This is a [[dynamic-equilibrium]]: *dynamic* because both reactions are
still continuing, with the forward rate equal to the reverse rate, and
*equilibrium* because the total amounts — the concentrations — of
reactants and products are now constant.

The sealed container is not optional. Remove the yellow squares as soon
as they form and they never get the chance to turn blue again: what was
a reversible reaction now runs entirely one way, blue turning yellow
with nothing to replace it. The same logic ends the section with a
mineral example. Consider the reversible decomposition of calcium
carbonate:

CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g)

If this were not done in a closed container, all the CO2 would escape
and the reverse reaction would not occur. Reversible reactions will
eventually reach a state of equilibrium if they are left in a sealed
container — that is the track's anchor statement, and every industrial
application later in the chapter depends on it.

:::key-point
Picture 64 blue squares each with a one-in-four chance per second of
flipping: 16 flip first, then 12 of the remaining 48, then 9 of the
remaining 36. The rate of change falls as the concentration of blue
squares falls — and the mirror-image rise of the reverse change means
the two rates must eventually become equal.
:::

:::misconception
"At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products are
equal." They are **constant**, not equal — the exact wording the exam
watches for. The blue-yellow model proves the difference: when the
rates match, the mixture typically holds far more of one form than the
other, yet the totals no longer change. Equal amounts would be a
coincidence, not a requirement; constant amounts are the definition.
:::

:::exam-hint
Definitions in this section are two-mark constructions. For dynamic
equilibrium: one mark for the forward and reverse reactions occurring
at the same rate, one mark for the concentrations of reactants and
products remaining constant. For the sealed container: no substances
added or able to escape. Write both halves every time — answers that
say only "the reactions balance" drop the concentration half, and
answers that say only "concentrations stop changing" drop the rates
half.
:::

:::quick-check
Rebuild the argument in five beats: what a sealed container allows and
blocks; why the blue-to-yellow rate starts high and falls; why the
yellow-to-blue rate starts at zero and rises; what is true at the
moment the rates meet; and why removing product as it forms destroys
the equilibrium. Then check yourself against the calcium carbonate
equation — which species escaping is what prevents its reverse
reaction?
:::

sections.title: The position of equilibrium
sections.markdown:
Take a general case where A reacts reversibly to give B:

A ⇌ 2B

The reaction from A to B — the left-to-right reaction — is described as
the [[forward-reaction]]. The reaction from B to A — the right-to-left
reaction — is called the [[reverse-reaction]]. Left and right here mean
exactly what they show on the page: reactants on the left of the arrow,
products on the right, and the double arrow in between promising that
both directions run.

Now let the mixture reach equilibrium and measure how much of each
substance is present. Suppose the measurement finds more A than B.
Because there is more A than B at equilibrium, we say that the
[[position-of-equilibrium]] lies to the left. The position is not a
place — it is a statement about which side of the equation dominates
the equilibrium mixture. Had the measurement found more B, the position
would lie to the right.

It is important to realise that equilibrium does not mean 50% reactants
and 50% products. The key thing is that the concentrations of A and B
stay constant at equilibrium — however lopsided the split. Those
constant concentrations will remain as they are until we change the
conditions, for instance the temperature or the pressure.

Watch what a condition change does. Increase the temperature and allow
the reaction time to reach equilibrium again, and the new measurement
might find less A and more B than before. Because the change decreased
the concentration of what is on the left and increased the concentration
of what is on the right, we say the position of equilibrium has shifted
to the right. Notice the subtlety: it does not matter that we still have
more A than B overall. What we look at is how things *changed* when we
changed the conditions — a shift is a movement, not an arrival.

One boundary case is worth pinning down now, because the next section
leans on it. The particles in solids and liquids are very close
together, and they are affected very little by changes in pressure;
their concentration does not really change as the pressure changes.
Pressure is a lever on gases — on the number of gas molecules in a given
volume — and the next two sections use exactly that picture to predict
which way any equilibrium moves.

:::key-point
The position of equilibrium describes which side dominates the mixture:
more A than B at equilibrium means the position lies to the left.
Equilibrium never means 50% on each side — the requirement is constant
concentrations, and a shift means the concentrations changed when the
conditions did.
:::

:::misconception
"The position of equilibrium lies where the amounts are equal."
Equilibrium positions are usually lopsided — the A ⇌ 2B example holds
more A than B, and that is a perfectly good equilibrium. What makes it
an equilibrium is that the lopsided split stays constant until
conditions change. When examiners ask "which side does the position
lie?", they want more-of/less-of language, never a fifty-fifty
assumption.
:::

:::exam-hint
Shift questions are marked on the *direction of change*, not the final
amount. If a temperature rise moves the mixture from "more A than B" to
"less A and more B", the position shifted right — even though A is
still the majority. Saying "the position moved right because the amount
of B increased and the amount of A decreased" earns the reasoning mark;
saying "there is now more B than A" would be wrong on the same facts.
:::

:::quick-check
Define the forward and reverse directions for A ⇌ 2B. If an equilibrium
mixture contains more B than A, which way does the position lie — and
what would we say after a condition change that produced less B and
more A? Finally, state why pressure changes barely affect solids and
liquids. Those three answers are the entire grammar of the next two
sections.
:::

sections.title: Predicting the effect of changing conditions
sections.markdown:
This section looks at what can be done to change the
[[position-of-equilibrium]] to produce as much as possible of what you
want in the equilibrium mixture. When the conditions in a system in
dynamic equilibrium are changed — for example the temperature or the
pressure — the position of equilibrium might shift left or right,
giving less or more of the products.

There is one master rule for predicting the direction. When conditions
change, the reaction always sets about counteracting the change you
made. It works like choosing clothes: if a room is too warm you take
off your jacket so you can cool down; if the room is too cold you put
more clothes on. The equilibrium mixture behaves the same way — every
shift you will ever predict is the reaction undoing your change as far
as it can.

The levers we might pull to influence the reaction are: changing the
pressure, changing the temperature, and adding a catalyst — which turns
out to have no effect on the position of equilibrium at all (the
catalyst gets its own section shortly). Before applying the pressure
lever, note its scope: the prediction only really applies to reactions
in which at least one of the reactants or products is a gas, and where
the total numbers of gaseous molecules on the two sides of the equation
are different.

Pressure is caused by molecules hitting the walls of their container;
fewer molecules in the same volume at the same temperature means lower
pressure. Take the general gas reaction:

A(g) + 2B(g) ⇌ C(g) + D(g)

There are three gaseous molecules on the left but only two on the
right. If you increase the pressure, the reaction responds by reducing
it again — and it can reduce the pressure by producing fewer gaseous
molecules to hit the walls, converting A + 2B (three molecules) into
C + D (two molecules). Increasing the pressure will always cause the
position of equilibrium to shift in the direction which produces the
smaller number of gaseous molecules.

The classic application is ammonia. Consider the reaction between
nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas:

N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g)

If we want to make as much ammonia as possible — to raise the
[[yield]] — we need to make the pressure as high as possible. There are
four molecules of gas on the left-hand side but only two on the
right-hand side, so increasing the pressure shifts the position of
equilibrium to the right: the ammonia side, the side with fewer gas
molecules.

The boundary case completes the rule. If there is the same number of
gaseous molecules on both sides of the equation, changing the pressure
makes no difference to the position of equilibrium. For example:

H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

Here increasing or decreasing the pressure has no effect on the
position of equilibrium — the amount of hydrogen iodide present at
equilibrium stays the same. Three molecules against three: nothing for
the reaction to gain by either direction, so the position stands still.
And remember from s05 why solids and liquids never join this
accounting: their particles are already packed close, so squeezing the
container changes their concentration hardly at all.

:::key-point
At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate
of the reverse reaction, so as much heat is being given out as is taken
in — nothing appears to change.
:::

:::key-point
In an endothermic reaction the heat is converted to a different form
(chemical energy), so it is being removed. That is why raising the
temperature pulls the position of equilibrium in the endothermic
direction, and why lowering it pushes the exothermic direction — the
mixture always works to counteract your change.
:::

:::did-you-know
The counteract rule you just learned is the working tool of industrial
chemistry. The ammonia synthesis above is carried out under high
pressure precisely because the equilibrium rewards high pressure with
more product — and the same rule, applied in reverse, tells engineers
which reactions gain nothing from squeezing. One sentence of prediction
logic, entire plant designs.
:::

:::misconception
"Increasing the pressure speeds everything up, so it also gives more
product." Pressure and rate are the last chapter's story; position is
this chapter's. For an equilibrium with equal gas-molecule counts on
both sides, a pressure change leaves the position of equilibrium
untouched even though the mixture is compressed. The prediction needs
the molecule count — three-against-two shifts, three-against-three
does not.
:::

:::exam-hint
Prediction questions are marked in two steps: state the direction
("shifts right / towards ammonia"), then give the counteract reason
("the right-hand side has fewer gas molecules, which reduces the
pressure"). Quote molecule counts from the balancing — four against two
for the ammonia reaction — because the number is the evidence. If the
counts are equal, say so and state that there is no effect; "no change"
with the equal-counts reason is a full-mark answer, not a refusal.
:::

:::quick-check
State the counteract rule in your own words, then apply it: for
A(g) + 2B(g) ⇌ C(g) + D(g), which way does the position move if the
pressure is increased, and why? Do the same for N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌
2NH3(g), quoting the molecule counts. Finally, explain why H2(g) +
I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) refuses to shift either way under pressure.
:::

sections.title: Temperature changes and catalysts
sections.markdown:
Two summary lines close the pressure account. Increasing pressure: the
[[position-of-equilibrium]] shifts to the side which has fewer gas
molecules. Decreasing pressure: the position of equilibrium shifts to
the side which has more gas molecules. One sentence each, both read
straight off the balancing of the equation.

Temperature needs one preparatory idea first. When we write a
reversible reaction showing an enthalpy change, the ∆H always shows the
enthalpy change for the [[forward-reaction]] — the value is given as if
the reaction were a one-way process. Take the general example:

A + 2B ⇌ C + D   ∆H = −100 kJ/mol

The ∆H being negative tells us the forward reaction is exothermic. The
[[reverse-reaction]] will be endothermic — by exactly the same amount.
Every reversible equation you meet comes with this built-in pairing:
one direction releases the heat, the other absorbs it, and the sign
written with the equation names which is which.

Now predict with the counteract rule. Suppose you change the conditions
by decreasing the temperature of an equilibrium — for example the
mixture is in equilibrium at 500 °C and you lower it to 100 °C. The
reaction will respond in a way that increases the temperature again.
How? If some A and B are converted into C and D, heat is given out,
because that is the exothermic change; the extra heat warms the
reaction mixture up again. So decreasing the temperature moves the
position of equilibrium to the right-hand side, and more C and D are
formed. You can watch it in the composition: this example's equilibrium
mixture at 500 °C is 80% reactants (A and B) and 20% products (C and
D); cooled to 100 °C and left to re-establish, it becomes 60% reactants
and 40% products. The product share grew exactly as the
rightward-shift demands.

Increasing the temperature has exactly the opposite effect. The
reaction equilibrium changes to remove the extra heat by absorbing it
in an endothermic change — this time the reverse reaction is favoured
and the position of equilibrium moves to the left. The summary lines
for the whole chapter: increasing temperature, the position of
equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction; decreasing
temperature, it shifts in the exothermic direction.

Which brings the chapter to its third lever. Adding a catalyst speeds
up reactions — and in a reversible change it speeds up the forward and
reverse reactions by the same proportion. If a catalyst speeds up the
forward reaction ten times, it speeds up the reverse reaction ten times
as well. The net effect: no change in the position of equilibrium if
you add a catalyst. Both rates rise together, so the point where they
meet — the equilibrium itself — keeps exactly the same composition. The
catalyst is added to increase the *rate at which equilibrium is
reached*: the same destination, reached sooner. That is why industrial
plants can afford catalysts — they never change how much product the
equilibrium holds, only how fast the mixture gets there.

:::key-point
∆H attached to a reversible equation belongs to the forward reaction
alone: A + 2B ⇌ C + D with ∆H = −100 kJ/mol means the forward reaction
is exothermic and the reverse reaction is endothermic by exactly the
same amount.
:::

:::misconception
"A catalyst increases the yield of a reversible reaction." It never
does — and this exam loves the distinction. The catalyst speeds both
directions by the same proportion, so the equilibrium composition is
untouched; what improves is the *time* taken to reach it. Yield belongs
to temperature and pressure; speed belongs to the catalyst. Answers
that promise extra product from a catalyst hand back the mark.
:::

:::exam-hint
Colour-change predictions need extra care. If you increase the pressure
on a coloured gas equilibrium, you squeeze the same number of molecules
into a smaller space, so the colour darkens *initially*; then it fades
a bit as the equilibrium re-establishes — but not back to its original
colour, because the gases are still compressed. Two-phase answers
(immediate effect, then the shift's partial correction) are what the
mark scheme rewards; single-phase answers miss the first phase.
:::

:::quick-check
For an exothermic forward reaction, state which way the position moves
when temperature rises and when it falls — quoting the endothermic/
exothermic rule each time. Then verify the 500 °C → 100 °C example: if
the product share rose from 20% to 40%, which direction shifted? Finish
by explaining, in the same-proportion language, why a catalyst leaves
the position of equilibrium exactly where it was.
:::

sections.title: Nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide
sections.markdown:
Nitrogen dioxide, NO2, is a dark brown, poisonous gas. It can
[[dimerise]] — join together in pairs — to make molecules of dinitrogen
tetroxide, N2O4, which is colourless. There is a
[[dynamic-equilibrium]] between the two forms:

2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g)

Every prediction rule from the last two sections now runs on one visible
mixture, because the two sides of this equation have different colours
and different molecule counts.

**Pressure.** If you increase the pressure, the position of equilibrium
will shift to reduce it again — by producing fewer gaseous molecules.
Two molecules on the left, one on the right, so the position of
equilibrium moves to the right and the mixture produces more
dinitrogen tetroxide, losing brown colour. If you lower the pressure,
the position of equilibrium shifts to increase the pressure again by
producing more gaseous molecules — it moves to the left, and you obtain
a higher proportion of the brown nitrogen dioxide in the equilibrium
mixture.

**Temperature.** Notice from the equation that the change from nitrogen
dioxide to dinitrogen tetroxide is exothermic: the negative sign for
∆H shows that heat is given out by the forward reaction. If you
decrease the temperature, the position of equilibrium shifts to produce
more heat to counteract the change — it moves in the exothermic
direction, so there is more dinitrogen tetroxide in the equilibrium
mixture and the colour of the reaction mixture fades. If you increase
the temperature, the position of equilibrium shifts to lower the
temperature again — it moves in the reverse, endothermic direction, more
nitrogen dioxide is formed, and the colour of the gas darkens.

**Reading the tubes.** The prediction can be seen directly. Take three
tubes containing this equilibrium mixture: one at lab temperature, one
standing in ice, one in hot water. The hot tube is very dark brown — a
high proportion of nitrogen dioxide, exactly as the endothermic
left-shift under heating demands. The tube in the ice is slightly
paler than the one in the open air, showing that cooling must have
given it a slightly greater proportion of the colourless dinitrogen
tetroxide. Notice the word *slightly*: the ice tube shifted left, but
only a little — equilibrium shifts counteract changes, they do not
flip the mixture.

One caution completes the section. The forward reaction here gives out
heat, so the reverse reaction takes it in — by exactly the same amount,
as always. Whichever way you push this mixture, the composition answers
by moving the colour: darker for more nitrogen dioxide, paler for more
dinitrogen tetroxide. Brown and pale are the readout of the
[[position-of-equilibrium]] itself.

:::misconception
"Cooling the tubes should make the colour disappear if dinitrogen
tetroxide is colourless." The shift is partial. The ice tube is only
*slightly* paler than the lab-temperature tube: cooling moved the
position of equilibrium towards the colourless side, but the mixture
still contains plenty of brown nitrogen dioxide. A shift changes the
proportions — it does not drain the reactant away, because the forward
and reverse reactions are both still running at their new common rate.
:::

:::exam-hint
This reaction is the examiner's favourite equilibrium story because one
mark sits on the molecule count (2 against 1) and one on the ∆H sign.
Write the equation first, annotate "2 → 1 molecules" beside it and
"forward exothermic" under it, and every pressure/temperature question
becomes a two-line quotation of s06's rules applied to those
annotations. The visible colour change is your built-in answer check:
darken means more NO2, fade means more N2O4.
:::

:::quick-check
Write the equilibrium equation, then predict and explain the colour
change for each of: increasing pressure, decreasing pressure,
increasing temperature, cooling in ice. Check each answer against the
tube observations — hot very dark, ice slightly paler than air. If any
prediction contradicts a tube, the error is in your molecule count or
∆H sign, and you can repair it from those two facts alone.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 21 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete equilibrium toolkit: the ⇌ arrow and what it
promises; the two named reversible reactions with their equations and
their heat directions; the sealed-container route to dynamic
equilibrium, with both of its defining characteristics; the position of
equilibrium and its left/right language; and the three levers —
pressure read from molecule counts, temperature read from the ∆H sign,
and the catalyst that changes neither. The nitrogen dioxide system
straps a colour readout onto all of it, so every shift has a visible
answer. The question bank for this chapter joins the platform by the
specification points below, so every practice item you are served
targets exactly the skills these sections taught.

Before you open the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's core
moves. Can you write both named reversible reactions — copper(II)
sulfate with its blue-white switch, ammonium chloride with its
disappearing-and-reappearing crystals — and say which direction needs
heat? Can you deliver the dynamic-equilibrium definition in its two
halves, rates equal and concentrations constant, and explain why the
container must be sealed? On the chemistry-only track: can you predict
a shift direction from a molecule count, from a ∆H sign, and state
plainly why a catalyst never moves the position? Anything that wobbled
is a section to revisit, not a reason to start over.

The bank itself trains four question shapes. Definition questions ask
what dynamic equilibrium means, with the marking note that *both*
words — dynamic and equilibrium — need explaining. Prediction tables
give several equilibria with their ∆H signs and ask which way the
position moves when temperature or pressure changes — the s06/s07
rules, one row at a time. Industrial questions run the full arc: a
reaction such as the reversible stage of the Contact process or the
methane-plus-steam route to hydrogen, with parts on defining the
equilibrium, choosing a pressure, and explaining what the catalyst does
for both the rate and the position. And the ammonia manufacture
question ties the whole chapter together — why high pressure raises the
conversion, why even higher pressure is not used (think risk), and why
the chosen temperature is a compromise that accepts less than the ideal
conversion. Practise all four shapes against the clock, and keep the
chapter's discipline: equation first, count the molecules, read the
sign, name the direction.

:::summary
- **Reversible reactions**: products can re-form the reactants;
  indicated by the ⇌ arrow. Named examples: dehydration of hydrated
  copper(II) sulfate (blue ⇌ white, heat in on dehydration, heat out on
  rehydration) and heating ammonium chloride (white solid ⇌ ammonia +
  hydrogen chloride gases, recombining where it is cooler).
- **Thermal decomposition**: the copper(II) sulfate forward change —
  one substance split into simpler substances by heat alone. The
  recombination step is acid (HCl) + base (NH3) making a salt.
- **Sealed container**: nothing added, nothing escapes (heat may pass).
  Reversible reactions reach equilibrium only in a closed system —
  escaping CO2 is why open-tube calcium carbonate decomposition never
  reverses.
- **Dynamic equilibrium**: forward and reverse reactions occur at the
  same rate AND the concentrations of reactants and products remain
  constant. Constant, never equal. The mixture keeps reacting —
  individual particles flip both ways forever.
- **Position of equilibrium**: which side dominates the mixture. Lies
  left if more reactant, right if more product; a *shift* is a change
  in the split when conditions change, not an arrival at 50/50.
- **Pressure**: shifts towards the side with fewer gas molecules
  (higher pressure) or more gas molecules (lower pressure). Equal
  molecule counts mean no effect. Solids and liquids are unaffected —
  their particles barely change concentration under pressure.
- **Temperature**: ∆H on the equation belongs to the forward reaction;
  the reverse is endothermic/exothermic by the same amount. Higher
  temperature shifts the endothermic direction; lower temperature the
  exothermic direction. Example: 80%/20% reactants/products at 500 °C
  became 60%/40% at 100 °C for the exothermic-forward A + 2B ⇌ C + D.
- **Catalysts**: speed forward and reverse by the same proportion — no
  change in the position of equilibrium; they shorten the time taken to
  reach it.
- **Model system**: 2NO2(g) ⇌ N2O4(g), brown ⇌ colourless; squeeze →
  paler (2 → 1 molecules), cool → paler (forward exothermic), heat →
  darker (reverse endothermic), with two-phase colour answers under
  compression.
:::

:::can-you
- State what the ⇌ symbol indicates in an equation?
- Describe both named reversible reactions — observations, equations,
  and which direction needs heat?
- Define dynamic equilibrium with both required halves, and explain why
  it needs a sealed container (calcium carbonate as the counterexample)?
- Say what the position of equilibrium means, and what a shift is —
  without assuming 50/50?
- Predict the direction of a pressure shift from molecule counts,
  including the equal-counts no-effect case?
- Predict the direction of a temperature shift from the ∆H sign,
  quoting the endothermic/exothermic rule?
- Explain why a catalyst does not affect the position of equilibrium,
  using the same-proportion wording?
- Read the NO2/N2O4 tube colours — including why the ice tube is only
  *slightly* paler?
:::

:::exam-hint
Past-paper items for this chapter cluster into four shapes: the
definition item (dynamic equilibrium, both words explained); the
prediction table (direction for each condition change, reasoned from
counts or ∆H); the industrial arc (Contact process, hydrogen from
methane and steam, ammonia — definition, then pressure, then catalyst
rate-and-position); and the colour-readout item with its two-phase
compression answer. The chemistry-only track means these appear on
Paper 2C; the definition and the two named reactions are core-track
marks. Practise the definition until its two halves are reflexes.
:::

:::misconception
"Once you know the rules, the named reactions are just trivia." The
named reactions are where the rules get *examined*. The copper(II)
sulfate switch carries the core-track marks and hands you a colour
readout for exothermic rehydration; the ammonium chloride tube tests
whether you can narrate a reversible change with its heat directions;
the calcium carbonate system is the standard sealed-container
counterexample. Every abstract rule in this chapter has one concrete
reaction attached — learn the pairs together and the rules stop being
abstract.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 3.17–3.22C chapter assessment items. Work
through the can-you list honestly, marking each item secure or shaky,
then take the platform's spec-joined question set for 3.20C and 3.22C
first — the two-half definition and the temperature/pressure
predictions earn the most marks per minute of chemistry-only revision,
and every one of them runs on rules you can quote from s04, s06 and
s07.
:::
